*Build the same presentation three ways, compare the results, and choose the right tool for the content and the data.*

## What you'll be able to do

- Turn an outline or document into a first-draft slide deck with an AI tool
- Compare three routes on the same content: Copilot Chat plus PowerPoint Designer, Adobe Express, and Claude Design
- Pick a tool based on what's in the slides, not just how they look
- Check an AI-built deck for wrong numbers, invented content, and accessibility problems

## Overview

AI slide tools are good at structure and layout: turning an outline into slides, suggesting designs, and making a deck look consistent. They are weak at substance. They pad slides with generic claims, invent statistics, and choose images that look right and mean nothing. Use them to get to a clean first draft, then do the part that matters yourself.

**Which tool depends on what's in the slides:**

| Tool | Drexel data rule | Best for | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Copilot Chat** (Drexel account) | High Risk Data when signed in with your Drexel account | Outlines, slide text, and speaker notes for internal decks | Writes the content; you paste it into PowerPoint. Copilot inside PowerPoint needs the paid Microsoft 365 Copilot license, which Drexel does not provide. |
| **PowerPoint Designer** | Part of Drexel's Microsoft 365 | Layouts for slides you've already written | Not Copilot, and available to everyone. Suggests layouts, not content. |
| **Adobe Express** | Moderate Risk Data | Public-facing talks, event and outreach presentations | Strong templates and images; approved by Drexel. |
| **Claude Design** (and similar tools such as Gamma) | **Low Risk Data only**; not Drexel-supported | Talks on published or public material | Often the most polished design. Never use it for internal, student, or unpublished research content. |
| **ChatGPT Edu** | Drexel ChatGPT Edu terms | Outlines, speaker notes, and restructuring | Can create a basic .pptx file, but design is plain. Best used to write the outline you feed to another tool. |

## Practice activities

Every activity uses the same public outline, built from published pedestrian-safety statistics. Verify the numbers against the original sources before you use them in a real talk.

> **Title:** Why Pedestrian Deaths Are Rising in U.S. Cities
>
> 1. The trend: U.S. pedestrian deaths rose about 18% from 2018 to 2022, the highest level since 1981.
> 2. Where: most deaths occur in urban areas, often on wide, fast arterial roads without sidewalks or crosswalks.
> 3. Who: Black and Hispanic pedestrians and adults 65 and older die at higher rates.
> 4. What works: road redesign (road diets, curb extensions, lower speed limits) has stronger evidence than education campaigns.
> 5. What's next: federal Safe Streets and Roads for All funding, and the local match barrier for under-resourced communities.
> 6. Call to action: prioritize street design in Vision Zero plans.

```{=html}
<details class="activity"><summary>Activity 1 · Novice — Write the slides in Copilot Chat, then lay them out with Designer</summary>
```

**Time** ~15 min · **Tools** Copilot Chat (Drexel account) or ChatGPT Edu, and PowerPoint with Designer

**Goal.** Build the deck with Drexel's own tools: AI writes the slide text, you paste it into PowerPoint, and Designer handles the layout.

**Steps.**

1. Open [Copilot Chat](https://m365.cloud.microsoft/chat) signed in with your Drexel account (or ChatGPT Edu) and type:

   > Turn this outline into slide text for a 7-slide presentation: a 15-minute talk to city planners. One title slide, then one slide per point. For each slide, give a title, no more than 4 short bullet points, and speaker notes with what to say. Use only the facts in the outline.

   Paste the outline after the prompt.
2. Open a blank presentation in PowerPoint. Paste each slide's title and bullets into a new slide, and the speaker notes into the **Notes** pane.
3. On each slide, open **Design → Designer** and pick a layout.
4. Save the deck as `version-powerpoint.pptx`.

**Expected result.** A working deck built entirely in Drexel-approved tools, with a plainer look than the other two versions.

**Check your work.** Did the AI add statistics or claims that weren't in the outline? Check every number before you paste it in.

```{=html}
</details>
```

```{=html}
<details class="activity"><summary>Activity 2 · Novice — Build the deck in Adobe Express</summary>
```

**Time** ~15 min · **Tools** Adobe Express (Drexel account)

**Goal.** See how a design-focused, Drexel-approved tool handles the same content.

**Steps.**

1. Sign in to Adobe Express with your Drexel account and start a new **presentation**.
2. Pick a template, or use the generative option and describe the talk: "15-minute talk for city planners on rising pedestrian deaths, clean and serious, data-focused."
3. Paste the outline content into the slides. Replace any stock images that are misleading (for example, a suburban sidewalk for a slide about urban arterials).
4. Export as PowerPoint or PDF and save as `version-express`.

**Expected result.** A more visually polished deck. Watch how much time goes into fixing template placeholder text and images.

**Check your work.** Look at every image and ask whether it shows what the slide claims. Generated or stock images of "pedestrians" often misrepresent the setting and the people most affected.

```{=html}
</details>
```

```{=html}
<details class="activity"><summary>Activity 3 · Novice — Build the deck in Claude Design (public content only)</summary>
```

**Time** ~15 min · **Tools** Claude Design (personal or PI-purchased Claude account; **Low Risk Data only**)

**Goal.** See what a leading non-Drexel design tool produces, and why the data rule limits where you can use it.

**Steps.**

1. Open Claude Design and describe the deck:

   > A 7-slide presentation for city planners on rising U.S. pedestrian deaths. Serious, clean, data-forward. One title slide, then one slide per outline point, with a simple chart for the trend on slide 2. Short text; the speaker will do the talking.

   Paste the outline.
2. Ask for one revision, for example: "Make the chart show only the 2018 and 2022 values, labeled."
3. Export to PowerPoint or PDF and save as `version-claude`.

**Expected result.** Often the most polished of the three. It may also be the most likely to add a chart with numbers you didn't provide.

**Check your work.** Check every value in any chart it draws. If you gave it two data points, a chart with ten is invented.

**Common pitfalls.** It is easy to paste something internal into a tool this convenient. Claude is Low Risk Data only: public, published material. No internal Drexel documents, student information, unpublished results, or draft grant content.

```{=html}
</details>
```

```{=html}
<details class="activity"><summary>Activity 4 · Novice — Compare and check the three versions</summary>
```

**Time** ~10 min · **Tools** The three decks

**Goal.** Choose a tool for your next real presentation.

**Steps.**

1. Put the three decks side by side. For each, note: time to a usable draft, number of factual fixes needed, number of image fixes needed, and how it looks.
2. Run PowerPoint's **Review → Check Accessibility** on each. Look for missing alt text, low color contrast, and slides without titles.
3. Decide which tool you'd use for (a) an internal department update, (b) a conference talk on published results, and (c) a community presentation.

**Expected result.** A tool choice driven by the content and data rules first, and design second. For internal content, that means Copilot Chat with PowerPoint, or Adobe Express.

```{=html}
</details>
```

## Data rules
Match the tool to what's in the slides. Copilot Chat signed in with your Drexel account is approved for High Risk Data; Adobe Express for Moderate Risk Data; Claude Design and other consumer tools for Low Risk Data only. See [Tools & Access](../tools.qmd) and Drexel's [AI Tools page](https://drexel.edu/provost/ai/tools).
:::
